story: Xuanzang recorded a reclining Buddha a thousand feet long sleeping somewhere beneath the valley — archaeologists still search for it; locals long called the standing pair Salsal and Shahmama, a petrified prince and princess of separated love.

name: Dhakeshwari National Temple
significance: The 'hidden goddess of Dhaka' who may have given the capital its name — since 1996 formally the National Temple of Bangladesh, centre of the country's Durga Puja and of Hindu public life. The original 800-year-old Dhakeshwari image was carried to Kolkata's Kumartuli in 1948, where it is still worshipped; the Dhaka shrine, damaged in 1971, was restored as the community's anchor.
story: Ballal Sena, the story runs, found an image of the goddess concealed (dhaka) in the jungle and enshrined her as Dhaka-Ishwari — the concealed sovereign lady from whom the megacity takes its name.

name: Kantajew Temple (Kantanagar)
significance: The finest terracotta temple of Bangladesh: every inch of its brick skin — some 15,000 plaques — narrates the epics, the Krishna lila, and the courtly life of 18th-century Bengal, from river barges to Portuguese muskets. Originally nine-spired, it lost its ratnas in the great 1897 earthquake yet remains the masterpiece of late Bengal temple art.
story: Its panels are read like a scroll by village storytellers at the Ras Mela — the annual fair when the deity travels by palanquin to Dinajpur town, a procession running unbroken since the Raj family's vow three centuries ago.

name: Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur
significance: The largest single Buddhist monastery south of the Himalaya — a quadrangle of 177 cells around a towering cruciform shrine whose terraced form, scholars argue, echoes across Bagan and even Angkor. A powerhouse of Pala-era learning tied to Nalanda and Vikramashila; the great teacher Atisha, who renewed Buddhism in Tibet, is associated with residence here. UNESCO-listed in 1985.
story: Its terracotta plaques mix Buddhas with snake-charmers, dancers and amorous couples — the monastery recording the whole world it renounced; Tibetan histories remember 'Somapuri' as one of the five jewel-viharas of the Pala realm.

name: Shwedagon Pagoda
deity: Relic stupa (eight hairs of the Buddha)
builtDisplay: raised to present form 14th–18th c.; origins far older
originNote: Mon foundations; legend places relics in the Buddha's lifetime
patron: Queen Shin Sawbu; King Dhammazedi; crown re-gilded by Mindon
significance: The golden heart of Myanmar: a 99 m stupa sheathed in genuine gold plates, its hti umbrella crusted with thousands of diamonds and rubies — enshrining, by tradition, eight hairs of the Buddha and relics of three predecessors, making it the oldest relic pagoda in Buddhist reckoning. Queen Shin Sawbu gave her weight in gold to gild it, beginning a national practice; every movement in Burmese history, royal or democratic, has rallied on this hill.
story: The merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika, first lay disciples, carried the Buddha's eight hairs home across the sea; opened on Singuttara hill, the casket blazed — the hairs rose, rays healing the blind and deaf, jewels raining — and the relics were sealed where the gods had kept the staff, water-filter and robe of three earlier Buddhas.
access: Yangon; four covered stairways & lifts; dress code, barefoot precinct.

name: Ananda Temple, Bagan
significance: The masterpiece among Bagan's 3,500+ monuments — a whitewashed Greek-cross temple crowned with a gilded sikhara, holding four 9.5 m standing Buddhas of the present aeon. The Kassapa image's smile changes with the viewer's distance — grave up close, radiant from afar. Restored with Indian ASI collaboration after the 2016 earthquake; Bagan entered the UNESCO list in 2019.
story: Eight monks from India described to Kyanzittha the Himalayan cave-temple of Nandamula; entranced, he built its likeness — then, the chronicle says, had the architect killed so it could never be duplicated: Bagan's dark parable of singular beauty.

name: Shwezigon Pagoda, Bagan
significance: The prototype of the Burmese stupa — the gilded bell whose form Shwedagon and a thousand others follow — built by Anawrahta, unifier of Burma and champion of Theravada. Crucially, he installed images of the 37 nats (spirits) here, absorbing the old animism into the new faith: the compact that still defines Burmese religion.
story: The site chose itself: a white elephant bearing the frontal-bone relic was set loose, and where it knelt the stupa rose — 'Shwezigon', golden hill of victory sand, where relic, kingship and the tamed nats met.

name: Mahamuni Buddha Temple
significance: Myanmar's most venerated image: the seated Mahamuni, carried over the mountains from Arakan (Mrauk-U) as war booty in 1785 — an act that still shapes Rakhine memory. Male devotees have applied so much gold leaf that the body lies under 15 cm of lumpy gold; each dawn a senior monk washes the image's face and brushes its teeth before crowds, the country's most intimate daily rite.
story: The Buddha himself, visiting Arakan, is said to have breathed life onto the casting — 'my brother' he called it, promising it would remain to represent him for five thousand years; only the face is left ungilded, kept mirror-bright by the morning ablutions.

name: Kyaiktiyo Pagoda (Golden Rock)
significance: A gilded granite boulder poised impossibly on the brow of a cliff, crowned by a 7.3 m stupa — one of Buddhism's three holiest sites in Myanmar with Shwedagon and Mahamuni. Pilgrims cross a bridge to press gold leaf onto the rock (men only may touch it); the boulder visibly rocks yet never falls.
story: The hermit Taik Tha kept a hair of the Buddha hidden in his own hair-knot for a lifetime, yielding it to the king only on condition it rest in a rock shaped like his head; Thagyamin, king of the gods, found this boulder on the ocean floor — the hair beneath it, they say, is all that keeps it from the abyss.

name: Wat Phra Kaew (Temple of the Emerald Buddha)
native: วัดพระแก้ว
significance: Thailand's palladium: the 66 cm jadeite Buddha, discovered in 1434 when lightning split a Chiang Rai stupa, travelled through Lampang, Chiang Mai and two centuries in Laos before Rama I enshrined it in his new Bangkok. The King of Thailand himself changes its gold seasonal robes thrice yearly; no other hand may touch it. The surrounding gallery holds the 178-panel Ramakien — Thailand's Ramayana — in mural form.
story: The image, legend claims, was fashioned in India by the gods' craftsman for the sage Nagasena, who prophesied it would carry Buddhism to five lands; wherever the Emerald Buddha resides, sovereignty and rain follow — which is why Laos and Siam contested it for centuries.
access: Grand Palace complex; strict dress code.

name: Wat Arun (Temple of Dawn)
builtDisplay: great prang raised under Rama II–III
significance: Bangkok's river icon: a 70–80 m Khmer-style prang sheathed in flowers of broken Chinese porcelain — ballast from trade junks turned to ornament — representing Mount Meru rising from the ocean. King Taksin reached this temple at dawn in 1767 after Ayutthaya's fall and made it home to the Emerald Buddha before Bangkok proper was founded across the river.
story: Named for Aruna, the Indian dawn-god and charioteer of the sun — the Hindu cosmos embedded in a Buddhist skyline; Indra on Erawan, the three-headed elephant, rides the prang's second terrace.

name: Wat Pho (Reclining Buddha)
significance: Bangkok's oldest and largest wat: the 46 m gold-leafed Reclining Buddha entering nirvana, feet inlaid with 108 mother-of-pearl auspicious signs. Rama III turned the cloisters into an open university — over a thousand inscriptions of medicine, massage and letters, now in UNESCO's Memory of the World — making Wat Pho the cradle of traditional Thai massage, still taught on site.
story: Dropping 108 coins in the 108 bronze bowls along the great image's back, pilgrims count off the Buddha's virtues — merit made audible, coin by coin, down the length of the sleeping giant.

name: Prasat Phanom Rung
significance: A Shaiva temple-mountain on the rim of an extinct volcano in Thailand's Khmer corridor, aligned so that at four moments a year the rising or setting sun pierces all fifteen doorways in a single shaft. The repatriation of its stolen Phra Narai (reclining Vishnu) lintel from the Art Institute of Chicago in 1988 became a national cause célèbre and a landmark of heritage return.
story: The sanctuary maps Shiva's Kailasa onto the volcano: the processional way crosses naga bridges — the passage from the human world across the cosmic ocean — before the mountain-summit sanctum where the hermit-prince Narendraditya retired as an ascetic.

name: Prasat Hin Phimai
significance: The largest Khmer temple in Thailand and terminus of the Ancient Khmer Highway from Angkor — 225 km of road, bridges and hospitals whose ceremonial gate faces Angkor itself. Built slightly before Angkor Wat, its central prang is widely seen as a design ancestor of that masterpiece; unusually for the empire, its heart is Tantric-Mahayana Buddhist.
story: Local legend weaves Phimai into the tale of Pachit and Oraphim — lovers whose trials named towns across the Khorat plateau; the temple's Buddhist dancer-lintels over Hindu doorframes record two faiths sharing one cosmology.

name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
significance: The mountain shrine of the North, its gilded chedi flashing over Chiang Mai from 1,000 m up Doi Suthep. Reached by a 306-step naga stairway; the road up was built in 1935 by tens of thousands of volunteers summoned by the charismatic monk Khruba Siwichai, finishing in under six months — northern Thailand's proudest act of collective merit.
story: A relic of the Buddha, brought north, miraculously doubled; one half was mounted on a white elephant let loose to choose its shrine — the beast climbed Doi Suthep, trumpeted three times, knelt and died: the chedi rose where it fell.

name: Angkor Wat
significance: The largest religious monument ever built — 162 hectares of moat, gallery and tower raised by Suryavarman II to Vishnu, its five peaks the mountain Meru, its bas-reliefs (including the 49 m Churning of the Ocean of Milk) the epics in stone. Uniquely west-facing; never wholly abandoned, it passed into Theravada worship and onto Cambodia's flag — the only building on any national flag. Angkor was UNESCO-listed in 1992 and is managed by the APSARA authority.
story: Khmer legend makes Angkor Wat the work of the divine architect Preah Pisnukar, built in a single night for the god-king; the moat is the cosmic ocean, and walking the west causeway at equinox one sees the sun rise exactly over the central tower — the universe re-centred each year.
access: Siem Reap ~6 km; Angkor Pass tickets; sunrise at the north pond is the classic darshan.

name: Bayon Temple, Angkor Thom
significance: State temple of Jayavarman VII, the empire's great Buddhist king — a forest of towers carved with over 200 colossal serene faces, compassion gazing to every horizon. Its outer galleries, uniquely, depict ordinary Khmer life — markets, cockfights, childbirth — beside the naval battle with the Chams that framed the king's rise.
story: The faces fuse Avalokiteshvara with Jayavarman himself — the bodhisattva-king watching all his people at once; stand anywhere in the Bayon and at least one face meets your eyes, the architectural claim that compassion has no blind spot.

name: Banteay Srei
significance: The 'Citadel of Women' — a miniature temple in rose-pink sandstone carved so deeply and finely it is called the jewel of Khmer art, and the rare great foundation built not by a king but by a scholar-priest, Yajnavaraha. Its pediments narrate Shiva's mythology with unmatched delicacy; the 1923 attempted theft of its apsaras by young André Malraux — future French culture minister — is one of art history's great scandals.
story: So fine is the carving that legend insisted no man's hand could have done it — the temple, people said, was carved by women; its guardian monkey-figures and the burning of Khandava forest pediment are keystones of Khmer myth in stone.

name: Ta Prohm
significance: The monastery Jayavarman VII dedicated to his mother as Prajnaparamita, goddess of wisdom — its stele records 12,640 residents and 66,000 farmers supporting it. Left deliberately in the forest's embrace by French conservators, its strangler figs and silk-cotton roots pouring over the galleries made it the world's image of ruin and return; India's ASI has partnered in its conservation since 2004.
story: The stele's inscription mourns and hopes at once: 'By the virtue of this good work, may my mother, freed from the ocean of existence, attain Buddhahood' — filial love as architecture, now cradled by the very jungle it once ordered.

name: Preah Vihear Temple
significance: Shiva as Lord of the Summit: an 800 m processional axis of stairways and gopuras climbing to a sanctuary on a 525 m Dangrek cliff over the Cambodian plain — the most dramatically sited of all Khmer temples. Awarded to Cambodia by the ICJ in 1962 (reaffirmed 2013) and UNESCO-listed in 2008, it remains entangled in recurring Thai–Cambodian border tensions — sacred geography as live geopolitics.
story: Legend ties the founding relic to a lock of Shiva's hair; the temple rises through five gopuras — pilgrims ascending, level by level, from the world of men to the god's mountain throne at the edge of the sky.

name: Sambor Prei Kuk (Ishanapura)
significance: Ishanapura, capital of Chenla — the temple city that came two centuries before Angkor, its brick sanctuaries (including unique octagonal towers) showing Indian temple ideas taking Khmer root. Here the flying-palace reliefs and inscribed Sanskrit foundations document Southeast Asia's creative absorption of the Indic world; UNESCO-listed in 2017.
story: Chinese envoys of the Sui court described Isanavarman's audience hall and five-day court cycle — the first outside portrait of a Khmer royal capital, matching the brick towers still standing in the 'forest of temples' (prei kuk).

name: Vat Phou (Wat Phu)
builtDisplay: standing structures 11th–13th c.; site from 5th c.
significance: The holy mountain of the Mekong: Lingaparvata's summit is a natural linga, and from the 5th century (pre-Angkorian Shrestapura, among the oldest Indic sites in Southeast Asia) to the Khmer empire, kings built an axial sanctuary climbing toward it, fed by a sacred spring that still bathes the (now Buddhist) shrine. UNESCO-listed in 2001 with its ancient planned landscape.
story: Local tradition remembers a yearly rite in which the mountain-god was honoured with a great buffalo offering by the Lao kings of Champasak — the Indic mountain-linga absorbed into Lao Buddhist festival, still celebrated each February full moon.

name: Pha That Luang
significance: The national symbol of Laos — a gold-covered lotus-bud stupa raised by Setthathirath when he moved the Lan Xang capital to Vientiane, on a site tradition traces to an Ashokan-era relic mission. Sacked in the 19th century and restored under the French, it centres the That Luang festival each November full moon, when the whole nation processes with wax flower-castles.
story: Five monks returning from India, the chronicle says, brought the Buddha's breastbone and enshrined it here in the 3rd century BCE under a first stupa — Laos joining its origin to Ashoka's great relic diaspora.

name: My Son Sanctuary
significance: Holy valley of the Cham kings for nine centuries — the longest continuously developed Indic sacred site in Southeast Asia, where each dynasty added brick kalan towers to Bhadresvara, the linga fusing king and god. The Chams' mortarless fired-brick technique still defies full explanation. B-52 carpet bombing in 1969 cratered the finest group; UNESCO listed the survivors in 1999.
story: Cham legend and inscription fuse founder-king Bhadravarman with Shiva as one name — Bhadresvara — the earliest royal linga cult of its kind in Southeast Asia, seeding the god-king idea Angkor would monumentalise.

name: Po Nagar Towers
deity: Yan Po Nagar (Bhagavati / Thien Y A Na)
significance: The goddess-temple of the southern Cham realm above the Cai river mouth — a 23 m brick tower to Yan Po Nagar, mother of the kingdom, identified with Bhagavati. Uniquely, worship never stopped changing hands: Vietnamese devotees today honour the same image as the goddess Thien Y A Na, incense unbroken across the transfer of civilisations.
story: Po Nagar, the Cham mother-goddess, taught the people rice and weaving; the Vietnamese retelling makes her a sandalwood spirit-girl who floated to China, wed a prince, and returned home in the fragrant log — one goddess, two peoples, one shrine.

name: Batu Caves Sri Subramaniar Temple
significance: The great Murugan shrine of the Tamil diaspora: a limestone cathedral-cave reached by 272 rainbow-painted steps beneath the world's tallest Murugan statue (42.7 m, gilded 2006). At Thaipusam over a million devotees carry kavadi burdens and milk pots up the stairs — the largest Hindu festival gathering outside South Asia.
story: Founder Thamboosamy Pillai, struck by the cave mouth's shape — the point of Murugan's vel — installed the deity in 1891; the god of Tamil hills thus claimed a Malaysian hill, and indentured-labour descendants made it their Palani across the sea.
access: 13 km north of KL; KTM Komuter Batu Caves station at the foot.

name: Sri Mahamariamman Temple, Kuala Lumpur
significance: The oldest functioning Hindu temple in Kuala Lumpur, founded 1873 by the same Thamboosamy Pillai who later opened Batu Caves — mother-goddess protector of the early Tamil migrants. Its 22.9 m five-tiered gopuram of 228 deities rises straight out of Chinatown; the temple's silver chariot leads the Thaipusam procession to Batu Caves each year.
story: Mariamman, the rain-and-smallpox mother of Tamil villages, travelled with every ship of indentured labourers as guardian against disease in strange lands — her KL house began as their first refuge of last resort.

name: Bujang Valley (Candi Bukit Batu Pahat)
significance: Malaysia's cradle of civilisation: over 50 excavated candi of the ancient Kedah kingdom on the Straits trade route, trading with Pallava India and the Srivijayan world — Sanskrit inscriptions, Shaiva shrines and Buddhist stupas together. Candi Bukit Batu Pahat, reassembled on its riverside terrace, is the emblem; the Sungai Batu digs pushed local ironworking and monuments to the early centuries CE.
story: Tamil poetics knew this coast as Kadaram, prize of the Chola overseas expeditions — Rajendra Chola's fleet struck here in 1025, the rare moment an Indian empire crossed the ocean in force, remembered on both shores.

name: Kek Lok Si Temple
significance: The largest Buddhist temple complex in Malaysia, terraced up Penang Hill around the Ban Po Thar pagoda — Chinese octagonal base, Thai middle tiers, Burmese crown: three Buddhist worlds in one tower, mirroring Penang's port cosmopolitanism. The 36.5 m bronze Kuan Yin and Lunar New Year illumination of tens of thousands of lamps are Penang institutions.
story: The founding abbot chose Air Itam's hills for their resemblance to a crane spreading wings over water — geomancy and refuge combined: 'Kek Lok' is the Pure Land, Sukhavati, promised within sight of the migrant harbour below.

name: Sri Mariamman Temple, Singapore
significance: Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, founded in 1827 by Naraina Pillai — the Penang clerk who arrived with Raffles and became the settlement's first Indian community leader. A gazetted National Monument in the heart of Chinatown; its annual Theemithi fire-walking festival, when devotees cross burning coals for Draupadi, closes the Mariamman ritual year.
story: Pillai installed the goddess first in wood and attap on land granted for the new colony's Indian temple — Mariamman guarding migrants against epidemic in the port city, as she had in every village they left behind.

name: Borobudur
significance: The largest Buddhist monument in the world: a stone mandala-mountain of nine terraces, 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddhas, walking pilgrims from the world of desire through the world of forms to the formless summit stupa. Abandoned as Java turned to Islam, buried in ash, cleared under Raffles in 1814, and saved by the great UNESCO restoration of 1975–83; Vesak at Borobudur remains Indonesian Buddhism's central rite.
story: Javanese tradition names the divine architect Gunadharma, whose profile is traced in the Menoreh hills that watch the monument; the hidden 'Karmawibhangga' reliefs of cause and effect lie deliberately buried at the base — the law of karma literally underlying the whole mountain.
access: ~40 km from Yogyakarta; timed summit tickets via Borobudur Park.

name: Prambanan (Candi Rara Jonggrang)
significance: The greatest Hindu temple of Indonesia and Borobudur's counterpart across the plain — 240 shrines originally, the 47 m Shiva tower flanked by Brahma and Vishnu, ringed with Ramayana reliefs that the Ramayana Ballet still dances against the floodlit towers on full-moon nights. Raised by Rakai Pikatan as the Hindu answer of the Sanjaya line to the Sailendras' Borobudur; UNESCO-listed in 1991.
story: Prince Bandung Bondowoso, to win Rara Jonggrang, had to build a thousand temples in one night; when spirits neared success she had the village women pound rice to trick the cocks into crowing dawn. Enraged at 999, he cursed her to stone — the slender Durga in the north cell, the 'slender maiden' the complex is named for.

name: Pura Besakih (Mother Temple)
builtDisplay: complex grown over 700+ years; origins older
originNote: Attributed to Rsi Markandeya's mission to Bali
significance: The Mother Temple of Bali: 23 linked puras on Mount Agung's slope, axis of the island's mandala of temples, where every Balinese clan and kingdom keeps a shrine. The Eka Dasa Rudra — the once-a-century purification of the universe — was underway in 1963 when Agung erupted catastrophically; lava spared the temple by metres, read across Bali as the gods' own testimony.
story: The sage Markandeya, guided by a vision, buried the panca datu — five sacred metals — here to still the island's unquiet forces; on that buried offering the whole thousand-year edifice of Balinese Hinduism literally stands.

name: Pura Tanah Lot
significance: Bali's sea-rock icon: one of the chain of sea temples ringing the island's coast, each within sight of the next, established in the wanderings of the Javanese priest Nirartha as Majapahit's Hindu high culture took final refuge in Bali. Cut off at high tide, silhouetted at sunset, it is among the most photographed sacred sites in Asia; a third of the rock was quietly rebuilt in a 1980s Japanese-aided restoration.
story: Nirartha, resting on the rock, was challenged by the local priest; he meditated the rock loose from the land, set his sash upon the waves as sea snakes to guard it, and left them there — the striped kraits in the base caves are honoured as those guardians still.

name: Pura Luhur Uluwatu
significance: One of Bali's six sad kahyangan directional temples, on a 70 m sea cliff at the island's southwestern point — guarding Bali from the spirits of the ocean as the sun goes down. The kecak fire-dance performed at its clifftop amphitheatre each sunset, chanting the Ramayana's monkey army, is the island's signature ritual-theatre.
story: Here Nirartha ended his earthly wanderings, attaining moksha in a flash of light from the cliff — 'Ulu-watu', the headland's stone, holding the point where the priest of all Bali's sea temples left the world; the temple monkeys are held to guard his relics with famous mischief.

name: Dieng Plateau Temples (Arjuna group)
significance: The oldest surviving temples of Java, small stone candi standing in a volcanic caldera 2,000 m up — 'Di Hyang', abode of the gods, where Indian temple form first took Javanese root a century before Borobudur. Of perhaps 400 original shrines, eight remain among sulphur vents and coloured lakes, named by later tradition for wayang heroes: Arjuna, Bima, Gatotkaca, Srikandi.
story: Mist rolling over the caldera gave rise to the belief that this is where gods and ancestors meet; the annual ruwatan here shaves the dreadlocked 'gimbal' children of the plateau, releasing them from spirit-claims in a rite that predates and outlived the temples' own worship.

name: Azhagiya Manavala Perumal Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple in Uraiyur, the old Chola capital, counted among the 108 Divya Desams and traditionally listed second after Srirangam. Unusually, the goddess Kamalavalli holds precedence here over the presiding deity.
story: Vishnu is said to have come to Uraiyur as the bridegroom Azhagiya Manavalan to wed the Chola princess Kamalavalli, an incarnation of Lakshmi.

name: Uthamar Kovil
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams, notable as one of the few historic Indian temples where Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma are all enshrined with their consorts in a single complex.
story: Shiva, wandering as the alms-seeking Bhikshatana, is said to have been fed to fullness here by Lakshmi, who thus earned the name Poornavalli.

name: Pundarikakshan Perumal Temple
significance: A Pallava-built Divya Desam at Thiruvellarai north of Tiruchirappalli, praised by Periyalvar and Thirumangai Alvar; its rock-cut caves and inscriptions date to the 8th century, with construction completed under Dantivarman.
story: A legend tells of king Sibi following a white boar to this spot, where at sage Markandeya's word Vishnu appeared from a milk-filled pit to receive worship.

name: Sundararaja Perumal Temple, Anbil
significance: The Divya Desam of Anbil village near Tiruchirappalli, where Vishnu reclines as Sundararajan; it is praised in the Prabandham by Tirumalisai Alvar and counted among the reclining-Vishnu shrines of the south.
story: The sage Suthapa, cursed by Durvasa to live as a frog, is said to have been restored to his form here by Vishnu as Sundararajan.

name: Appakkudathaan Perumal Temple
significance: A reclining-Ranganatha Divya Desam at Koviladi on the Kaveri near Tiruchirappalli, and the only one of the 108 where the sweet neyyappam is offered to the deity every night.
story: Vishnu, disguised as a hungry old pilgrim, is said to have eaten king Upamanyu's entire food offering and been satisfied only by a pot of appam, lifting the king's curse.

name: Hara Saabha Vimocchana Perumal Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Thirukandiyur near Thiruvaiyaru, praised by Thirumangai Alvar and one of the few temples housing images of Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma in one premises.
story: Shiva, burdened by the sin of severing Brahma's fifth head, is said to have been freed of it after worshipping Vishnu and bathing in the temple tank here.

name: Jagad Rakshaka Perumal Temple
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams, on the Kaveri near Kumbakonam, where Vishnu is worshipped as Jagathrakshaka, protector of the world; later patronage came from Vijayanagara kings and the Madurai Nayaks.
story: Local tradition links the shrine to Varaha, the boar form in which Vishnu raised the earth goddess Bhumi from the netherworld.

name: Gajendra Varadha Perumal Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Kabisthalam near Papanasam, held to be where Vishnu rescued the elephant king Gajendra; it is also counted among the five Pancha-Kannan temples where Krishna receives special prominence.
story: When a crocodile seized the elephant Gajendra at the temple tank, Vishnu's discus is said to have freed both animals from their curses.

name: Thirupullabhoothangudi Temple (Valvil Ramar)
significance: A Divya Desam near Kumbakonam where Vishnu is worshipped as Valvil Ramar, uniquely depicted as Rama with four arms bearing the conch and discus.
story: Rama is believed to have performed the funeral rites of the eagle king Jatayu at this spot, with Bhudevi beside him in Sita's place.

name: Sarangapani Temple
significance: The great Vishnu temple of Kumbakonam and one of the foremost of the 108 Divya Desams, its central shrine shaped as a celestial chariot; the structure grew under the Cholas and was expanded through the Vijayanagara and Nayak eras.
story: Lakshmi is said to have emerged as Komalavalli from the Potramarai tank, and Vishnu to have descended as Aravamudhan to wed her.

name: Oppiliappan Temple
significance: A major Vaishnava pilgrimage shrine near Kumbakonam, counted 60th among the 108 Divya Desams and glorified in the Tamil canon; Chola-era in origin with additions by the Thanjavur Nayaks.
story: Vishnu is said to have asked the sage Markandeya for his foster daughter - Lakshmi raised beneath the tulasi - and married her at this place.

name: Nachiyar Kovil (Thirunarayur Nambi Temple)
significance: The Divya Desam of Thirunaraiyur near Kumbakonam, where the goddess Vanjulavalli ranks above Vishnu himself; its stone Garuda is famed for growing heavier as it is carried in procession. Tradition credits the original shrine to Kochengat Cholan.
story: Vishnu is said to have married Vanjulavalli, foster daughter of sage Medhavi, on the condition that she would always receive first honours.

name: Saranatha Perumal Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Tirucherai near Kumbakonam, unusual in giving Vishnu five consorts and in housing a shrine to the river goddess Kaveri; Chola inscriptions of the 10th century record endowments.
story: Vishnu is said to have appeared as a child to the goddess Kaveri here to test her devotion, then granted her rank equal to the Ganga.

name: Bhaktavatsala Perumal Temple
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams, at Thirukannamangai in Tiruvarur district, glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham; built under the later Cholas with Thanjavur Nayak additions.
story: Lakshmi, emerging from the churned Ocean of Milk, is said to have done penance here until Vishnu wed her as Bhaktavatsala.

name: Neelamegha Perumal Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Thirukannapuram in Nagapattinam district, second only to Srirangam in the number of Alvar hymns addressed to its presiding deity.
story: When a hair was found in a garland offered by the priest Rangabhatta, Vishnu is said to have appeared wearing a wig - sowri - to shield his devotee from blame, earning the name Sowriraja.

name: Loganatha Perumal Temple
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams, near Nagapattinam, where Vishnu presides as Loganatha behind a five-tier rajagopuram; later patronage came from Vijayanagara and Madurai Nayak rulers.
story: Krishna is said to have snatched sage Vasishtha's butter offering as a child and, chased to this spot, granted the assembled sages leave to dwell here forever.

name: Soundararajaperumal Temple, Nagapattinam
significance: The coastal Divya Desam of Nagapattinam, home to a rare eight-armed Narasimha image; the shrine goes back to the later Cholas with Nayak and Maratha additions.
story: Vishnu is held to have shown himself here across the ages - to sage Markandeya, to Dhruva, and to a Chola king in the Kali age.

name: Thanjai Mamani Koil
significance: A group of three adjacent Vishnu temples on the edge of Thanjavur that together form a single Divya Desam, an arrangement unique among the 108; patronage spanned the Cholas, Vijayanagara and the Madurai Nayaks.
story: The Brahmanda Purana tells of Vishnu slaying three demons here - Thanjakan among them - from whom Thanjavur is said to take its name.

name: Nathan Kovil (Thirunandhipura Vinnagaram)
significance: The Divya Desam of Thirunandhipura Vinnagaram near Kumbakonam, where Shiva's bull Nandi stands within the Vishnu sanctum - a rare joining of Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion. The Pallava king Nandivarman II is remembered as an ardent devotee.
story: Nandi, cursed by Vishnu's gatekeepers for disrespect, is said to have won release through penance at this shrine.

name: Kola Valvill Ramar Temple
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams, a village shrine 19 km from Kumbakonam where Vishnu is worshipped as the bow-bearing Kola Valvill Ramar, praised in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: The divine architect Mayan is said to have raised this temple by the Kaveri as an earthly Vaikuntha at Brahma's bidding.

name: Devaadi Raja Perumal Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Therazhundur in Mayiladuthurai district, whose deity Amaruviappan - the lord flanked by cattle - is traced by tradition to Karikala Chola's time, with 11th-century Chola additions.
story: Brahma, having driven off Krishna's cattle, is said to have begged pardon and asked the god to abide here, where the herds gathered around him.

name: Sthalasayana Perumal Temple, Tirusirupuliyur
significance: A small Divya Desam near Kollumangudi where Vishnu lies in a rare south-facing sleeping posture, one of only two such among the 108.
story: For the aged sages Vyaghrapada and Patanjali, Vishnu is said to have taken a small reclining form - Bala Sayanam - so their failing eyes could behold him.

name: Nanmadiya Perumal Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Thalachangadu near Akkur in Mayiladuthurai district, sung by Thirumangai Alvar and patronised by Chola kings.
story: Chandra the moon god, cursed by Brihaspati, is said to have worshipped Vishnu here and regained his light.

name: Parimala Ranganatha Perumal Temple
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams and one of the five Pancharanga Kshetrams of Ranganatha along the Kaveri, at Mayiladuthurai; patronage spanned the Cholas, Vijayanagara and the Madurai Nayaks.
story: The place-name Indalur recalls Indu, the moon, whose curse is said to have been lifted by Vishnu at this shrine.

name: Thirukkavalampadi
significance: One of the eleven Divya Desams clustered at Thirunangur near Sirkazhi, closely associated with Thirumangai Alvar, where Krishna is worshipped as Gopalakrishnan with Rukmini and Satyabhama.
story: Krishna and Satyabhama are said to have kept a garden at this spot, where the god once saved an elephant - the kavalam of its name.

name: Kazheesirama Vinnagaram
significance: The Divya Desam of Sirkazhi, where Vishnu presides as Trivikrama, the god who measured the worlds; Chola in origin with later Vijayanagara and Madurai Nayak work.
story: Vishnu as Trivikrama is said to have blessed the sage Romasa here with a lifespan outlasting Brahma's.

name: Thiruarimeya Vinnagaram
significance: One of the eleven Thirunangur Divya Desams near Sirkazhi, where Vishnu is worshipped as the pot-dancing Kudamudakoothan.
story: When Shiva's grief-stricken dance threatened the worlds, Vishnu is said to have appeared at Nangur in eleven forms to calm him - this shrine marks one of them.

name: Thiruvanpurushothamam
significance: One of the eleven Divya Desams of Thirunangur near Sirkazhi, sung by Thirumangai Alvar, with Vishnu enshrined as Purushottaman.
story: This shrine counts among the eleven forms Vishnu is said to have assumed at Nangur to still Shiva's dance of grief.

name: Perarulaalan Perumal Temple (Thirusemponsei Koil)
significance: The Divya Desam Thirusemponsei Koil, one of the eleven Vaishnava shrines of Thirunangur near Sirkazhi, housing Vishnu as Perarulalan, the greatly gracious.
story: After Shiva's dance of fury at Nangur, Vishnu is said to have appeared in eleven forms to calm him, this shrine among them.

name: Thirumanimadam
significance: One of the eleven Thirunangur Divya Desams, with Vishnu enshrined as Narayanan; inscriptions of the 10th-century Chola and later Nayak periods survive in the temple.
story: The shrine is counted among the eleven forms Vishnu assumed at Nangur to calm Shiva's grief-stricken dance.

name: Thiruvaikunda Vinnagaram
significance: One of the eleven Divya Desams at Thirunangur near Sirkazhi, where Vishnu presides as Vaikuntanathan, lord of Vaikuntha, glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: The temple marks one of the eleven forms Vishnu is said to have taken at Nangur to quell Shiva's wrathful dance.

name: Thiruvali-Thirunagari Temples
significance: Twin temples about 10 km from Sirkazhi that together count as a single Divya Desam, jointly addressed in all forty-one pasurams about the site and closely tied to the life of Thirumangai Alvar.
story: The deities of both shrines are believed to have revealed themselves to Thirumangai Alvar at this place.

name: Thiruthevanartthogai
significance: One of the eleven Divya Desams of Thirunangur near Sirkazhi, where Vishnu is worshipped as Deivanayagan with the goddess Kadalmagal.
story: The shrine is one of the eleven forms Vishnu is said to have assumed at Nangur, at Shiva's own request, to end his dance of grief.

name: Thiruthetriyambalam
significance: One of the eleven Thirunangur Divya Desams, with a reclining Ranganatha as its presiding deity; alone among the eleven it keeps both Rama and Krishna as festival deities.
story: Krishna is said to have appeared here as Parthasarathy to begin Arjuna's instruction, and the temple tank is remembered as Arjuna's digging.

name: Thirumanikkoodam
significance: One of the eleven Divya Desams at Thirunangur, with Varadharaja Perumal presiding; it is noted as the only Nangur shrine praised by Alvars besides Thirumangai.
story: Here too tradition tells of Krishna appearing as Parthasarathy to instruct Arjuna, who dug the temple tank.

name: Annan Perumal Koil (Thiruvellakulam)
significance: The Divya Desam of Thiruvellakulam near Sirkazhi, known as Annan Perumal Koil, one of the eleven Vaishnava shrines of the Thirunangur country revered by the Alvars.

name: Thiruppaarththanpalli
significance: One of the eleven Thirunangur Divya Desams east of Sirkazhi, where Vishnu is Taamaraiyaal Kelvan, beloved of the lotus lady; its shrine uniquely houses festival images of both Rama and Krishna together.
story: Arjuna is said to have dug the temple tank with a sword given by Krishna, who then appeared as Parthasarathy to begin his teaching here.

name: Devanathaswamy Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Thiruvahindrapuram near Cuddalore, the only historic South Indian temple with a hilltop Hayagriva shrine; over fifty inscriptions record Chola, Pandya and Vijayanagara patronage from Kulothunga I to Achyuta Deva Raya.
story: When Garuda delayed fetching sacred water, the serpent Adishesha is said to have struck open a well whose water still serves the daily rituals.

name: Ulagalantha Perumal Temple, Tirukoyilur
significance: The Divya Desam of Thirukkoyilur, where Vishnu stands as the Trivikrama who strode the three worlds; its granite structure took shape under Virarajendra Chola, and its 59-metre gopuram is the third tallest temple tower in Tamil Nadu.
story: Here Vamana the dwarf is said to have begged three paces of land from king Mahabali and grown to measure the universe.

name: Varadharaja Perumal Temple, Kanchipuram
significance: One of the holiest Vaishnava temples of India and a principal Divya Desam, at Chinna Kanchipuram; renovated by the Cholas in 1053 and enlarged through Vijayanagara times, its hundred-pillared hall is celebrated as a masterpiece of Vijayanagara architecture.
story: Vishnu is said to have blazed forth as Varadharaja from beneath the athi tree during Brahma's great sacrifice on this spot.

name: Ashtabujakaram
significance: One of the fourteen Divya Desams of Kanchipuram, where Vishnu bears eight arms and eight weapons; Pallava in origin with later Chola and Vijayanagara additions.
story: Vishnu is said to have taken his eight-armed form here to destroy a serpent sent to break Brahma's sacrifice.

name: Deepaprakasa Perumal Temple (Thiruthanka)
significance: The Divya Desam of Thiruthanka in Kanchipuram, seat of Deepaprakasa, the light-effulgent lord; its inscriptions run to the reign of Rajaraja Chola III, with later Vijayanagara patronage.
story: When Saraswati loosed darkness on Brahma's rite, Vishnu is said to have risen like lamplight to guard it, becoming Deepaprakasa.

name: Tiruvelukkai (Azhagiya Singar Temple)
significance: The smallest of Kanchipuram's Divya Desams, where Narasimha presides as Alagiya Singar; Pallava in origin with Chola and Vijayanagara additions, it drew praise from several Alvars and acharyas.
story: Vishnu is said to have taken the man-lion form Narhari here to guard Brahma's horse sacrifice from demons.

name: Thiruneeragam (Jagadeesha Perumal Shrine)
significance: One of four Divya Desams enshrined within the Ulagalantha Perumal Temple complex of Kanchipuram, whose earliest inscription dates to 846 CE; the temple began under the Pallavas with Chola, Vijayanagara and Nayak additions.

name: Pandava Thoothar Perumal Temple
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams and counted among the three oldest Vishnu temples of Kanchipuram, built by the Pallavas with Chola and Vijayanagara additions. It is celebrated for its unusually large seated image of Krishna as the Pandavas' envoy, and is hymned in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: Krishna, serving as the Pandavas' peace envoy, is said to have revealed his colossal cosmic form here when Duryodhana tried to trap him in a pit.

name: Nilathingal Thundam Perumal Temple
significance: A Divya Desam that stands inside the precinct of the Ekambareswarar Shiva temple, one of the very few Vishnu shrines of the 108 housed within a Shaiva complex. First raised under the Pallavas, it was rebuilt by the Cholas with later Vijayanagara-era additions.
story: Vishnu is said to have cooled Parvati's fiery penance here with rays reflected from the crescent moon on Shiva's head, earning the name Nilathingal Thundam.

name: Ulagalantha Perumal Temple (Thiruooragam)
significance: A Divya Desam housing a colossal image of Vishnu as Trivikrama striding the worlds, its earliest inscription dated 846 CE under Pallava Nandivarman III with later Chola development. Uniquely, the complex shelters four separate Divya Desams within one precinct.
story: Here Vamana the dwarf is said to have grown into cosmic Trivikrama, measuring the three worlds in two strides and humbling the generous king Mahabali with the third.

name: Yathothkari Perumal Temple (Thiruvekka)
significance: One of the three oldest Vishnu temples in Kanchipuram, believed to be a late 8th-century Pallava foundation with Chola and Vijayanagara additions. The Divya Desam is closely tied to the poet-saint Thirumalisai Alvar and is glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: The deity is said to have rolled up his serpent bed to follow the banished Thirumalisai Alvar out of the city, then returned 'as requested' - the meaning of Yathothkari.

name: Thirukkaragam (Karunakara Perumal shrine)
builtDisplay: within the Pallava-era Ulagalantha Perumal complex
significance: A Divya Desam in its own right, maintained as the Karunakara Perumal shrine on the third precinct of Kanchipuram's Ulagalantha Perumal temple complex, one of four Divya Desams sheltered there. The consort is worshipped as Padmamani Nachiyar.
story: The sage Garga is said to have won divine knowledge through penance here, giving the place its old name Garagaham, later Karakam.

name: Thirukkarvaanam (Kalvar Perumal shrine)
builtDisplay: within the Pallava-era Ulagalantha Perumal complex
significance: A Divya Desam preserved as the Kalvar shrine with consort Kamalvalli Thayar on the second precinct of the Ulagalantha Perumal temple complex, one of the four Divya Desams that share the compound. It is glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.

name: Thirukkalvanur (Adi Varaha Perumal shrine)
builtDisplay: attested among the Divya Desams; construction unrecorded
significance: A Divya Desam that survives as the Adi Varaha Perumal shrine within the premises of the Kamakshi Amman temple, beside the goddess's sanctum. Its Lakshmi image is unusual in facing the deity in a worshipping posture, and the shrine bears the Vamana vimana.

name: Pavalavannam Perumal Temple
significance: A Divya Desam attributed to the Cholas, carrying inscriptions of Rajadhiraja Chola and Kulothunga Chola I, with later Vijayanagara contributions. It forms a pair with the Pachaivannar temple standing axially across the road.
story: Vishnu is said to have assumed the hue called pavalam here in the Treta Yuga, and so came to be worshipped as Pavalavannar.

name: Vaikunta Perumal Temple (Thiru Parameswara Vinnagaram)
significance: An 8th-century royal foundation of Pallava Nandivarman II and a Divya Desam, whose stepped vimana with tiered sanctums provided a prototype for the far larger temples of later Tamil Nadu. Its sculpted cloister panels narrate Pallava history, and its study has even helped date portions of the Bhagavata Purana.
story: A child of sage Bharadvaja's line, granted by Vishnu to a childless Pallava king, is said to have grown to build this temple as king Parameswara.

name: Vijayaraghava Perumal Temple
significance: A Divya Desam near Kanchipuram believed to have been built by 13th-century Pandya kings, with later Chola and Thanjavur Nayak contributions. Rama is worshipped here as the victorious Vijayaraghava, and the temple is glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: Rama is said to have performed the funeral rites of the eagle-king Jatayu, who fell defending Sita, at the pit (kuzhi) that names this place.

name: Veeraraghava Swamy Temple
significance: A Divya Desam whose origins are placed in the late 8th-century Pallava period, though most scholars attribute the major surviving structures to 14th-century Vijayanagara kings. The deity is venerated as a divine healer, and the temple tank is the largest among the Divya Desams.
story: The sage Salihotra is said to have offered his only meal to Vishnu, who had come disguised as a guest and remained here to bless him, marrying Lakshmi at this spot.

name: Parthasarathy Temple
significance: One of the oldest structures in Chennai, this Divya Desam was raised by the Pallavas under Narasimhavarman and expanded by Chola and 15th-century Vijayanagara rulers. It uniquely houses five forms of Vishnu, with Krishna presiding as Parthasarathy, Arjuna's charioteer.
story: The face of the main image bears mark-like scars, believed to be Bhishma's arrows taken by Krishna while driving Arjuna's chariot in the Mahabharata war.

name: Thiruneermalai Temple Complex (Neervanna Perumal)
significance: A twin-site Divya Desam spread across a hill and its base near Chennai, carrying Chola- and Pandya-period inscriptions. Vishnu appears here in four postures - standing as Neervannan, reclining as Ranganatha, sitting as Narasimha and walking as Trivikrama.
story: The sage Valmiki is said to have worshipped Ranganatha on the hilltop after composing the Ramayana and to have met Rama himself at its base.

name: Nithyakalyana Perumal Temple
significance: A coastal Divya Desam on the Mahabalipuram road whose original structure was raised by the 7th-century Pallavas with 11th-century Chola additions. Its sanctum holds a rare seven-foot granite Varaha bearing Bhudevi on his lap, and the shrine is favoured by those seeking marriage.
story: Varaha is said to have wedded the 360 daughters of the sage Kalava one on each day of the year, becoming the 'ever-marrying' Nithyakalyana Perumal.

name: Sthalasayana Perumal Temple (Thirukadalmallai)
significance: The Divya Desam of the UNESCO World Heritage port town of Mahabalipuram, where Vishnu reclines directly on the bare ground rather than on his serpent. Founded under the Pallavas, it was moved to its present site in the 14th century by the Vijayanagara king Parankusa.
story: Vishnu is said to have chosen to recline on the bare earth here so that the sage Pundarika's interrupted flower-worship would not go in vain.

name: Yoga Narasimha Temple (Thirukkadigai)
significance: A hilltop Divya Desam where Narasimha sits in yogic repose above Sholinghur, recorded in donations of Kulothunga Chola III among others. Tradition holds that worship lasting a single kadigai - twenty-four minutes - here yields the Lord's grace, giving the shrine its name.
story: The sage Vishvamitra is said to have won his title of Brahmarishi at this hill.

name: Thirunavaya Navamukunda Temple
builtDisplay: ancient; Mamankam venue from at least the 8th c.
significance: A Divya Desam on the Bharathappuzha river and the storied venue of the Mamankam, the great fair held once every twelve years from at least the 8th century CE. It remains one of Kerala's principal riverside shrines for ancestral rites.
story: Nine yogis are said to have installed images here; eight sank into the earth, and the ninth, arrested at its knees, became Navamukunda.

name: Thrikkakara Vamanamoorthy Temple
significance: A rare major temple dedicated to Vamana and a Kerala Divya Desam, regarded as the home of the Onam festival - its inscriptions carry the earliest known mention of Onam, dated 861 CE.
story: Here Vamana is said to have humbled King Mahabali with three cosmic strides, granting the devoted king an annual return to his people - the homecoming celebrated as Onam.

name: Thirumoozhikkulam Lakshmana Perumal Temple
significance: One of the thirteen Kerala Divya Desams and unusual in being dedicated to Lakshmana, with a circular granite-and-laterite sreekovil in classic Kerala style. It is also a station of the Nalambalam pilgrimage of the four Ramayana brothers.
story: Vishnu is said to have imparted the 'Thiru Mozhi', sacred words of guidance, to the sage Harita here, giving the place its name.

name: Sreevallabha Temple
significance: Among the largest and oldest temple complexes of Kerala and a Divya Desam, traditionally dated to 57 BCE and later brought under Travancore in the 1750s. It is famed for staging Kathakali nightly as a temple offering.
story: Vishnu is said to have come as a young celibate student to answer an aged devotee's prayers and slain the demon Thukalasura, before revealing his universal form.

name: Thrikodithanam Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Kerala Divya Desam hymned by Nammalvar and counted among the five ancient shrines of the Pamba belt linked to the Pandava brothers, this one attributed to Sahadeva.
story: After crowning Parikshit, the five Pandavas are said to have each raised a shrine on their last pilgrimage; Sahadeva installed the image worshipped here.

name: Thrichittatt Mahavishnu Temple
significance: Chief among the five Chengannur-area temples attributed to the Pandava brothers and a Divya Desam sung by Nammalvar around 800 CE, with stone inscriptions of the Second Chera empire.
story: Yudhishthira is said to have built this temple in penance for the half-truth he spoke to fell Drona in the Kurukshetra war.

name: Thripuliyoor Mahavishnu Temple (Thiruppuliyur)
significance: A Divya Desam of the Kuttanad tract glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, with inscriptions of the Second Chera empire; among the five Pandava temples of the region it is attributed to Bhima.
story: Bhima is said to have raised this shrine to Krishna during the Pandavas' final pilgrimage along the Pamba.

name: Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple
significance: A riverside Divya Desam on the Pamba, home of the spectacular Aranmula snake-boat race rowed during Onam and of the village craft of the Aranmula kannadi metal mirror. Among the Pandava shrines of the region it is linked to Arjuna.
story: Arjuna is said to have built the shrine in atonement for slaying the unarmed Karna, bringing the image on a raft of six bamboos - the 'aran-mula'.

name: Thiruvanvandoor Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Divya Desam glorified by Nammalvar with inscriptions of the Second Chera empire, counted among the five Pamba-belt temples of the Pandavas and attributed to Nakula.
story: Nakula is said to have installed the image here on the Pandavas' last pilgrimage after Parikshit's coronation.

name: Thiruvazhmarban Temple (Thiruvanparisaram)
significance: A Divya Desam near Nagercoil where Lakshmi is believed to dwell on the Lord's chest - the meaning of Thiruvazhmarban - traditionally founded by king Kulasekara, the Alvar, with its oldest inscription dated 1139 CE and a Nayak-era temple tank.
story: King Kulasekara is said to have found his lost horse grazing by the temple tank and, revived by its waters, raised the temple in gratitude.

name: Vaishnava Nambi Temple (Thirukkurungudi)
significance: The 'Dakshina Vaikuntam' Divya Desam at the foot of the Western Ghats, recorded in medieval Chola inscriptions from the 10th century onward. It is the home of the Kaisika Natakam temple-theatre tradition and of Arayar Sevai recital worship.
story: The Kaisika legend tells of the singer Nambaduvan, whose devotional song freed a demon of its curse while Nambi himself appeared to honour the humble devotee.

name: Vanamamalai Perumal Temple
significance: A Divya Desam believed to be a Pandya foundation with its earliest inscription of 1236 CE and later Vijayanagara and Madurai Nayak additions; it is revered as one of the eight svayambu (self-manifested) fields of Vishnu.
story: Adishesha and Garuda are both said to have done penance here, winning the honours of serving as Vishnu's couch and as the guardian of Vaikuntha.

name: Srivaikuntanathan Perumal Temple
significance: First of the nine Nava Tirupati temples strung along the Tamiraparani and a Divya Desam revered by Nammalvar, ranked next only to Alwarthirunagari among the nine; royal grants are recorded from Jatavarman Kulasekaran I (1190-1216) onward.
story: Vishnu is said to have slain the asura Somuka, who stole the four Vedas from Brahma, and then taken residence here as Vaikuntanatha.

name: Srinivasa (Mayakoothar) Perumal Temple
significance: The Nava Tirupati Divya Desam of Thirukkulandai, honoured as the Shani sthalam - the Saturn station - of the nine planetary temples of the Tamiraparani belt.
story: Vishnu is said to have crushed an abducting asura and danced upon his head as Koothar to restore the devotee Kumudhavalli to her husband.

name: Vaithamanidhi Perumal Temple
significance: The eighth of the Nava Tirupati Divya Desams, where the reclining lord is imagined as keeper of a buried treasure, and the birthplace of Madhurakavi Alvar, devoted disciple of Nammalvar. The present structure owes its refurbishment to Rani Mangammal of Madurai.
story: Kubera, cursed by Shiva, is said to have regained his lost wealth after penance before Vaithamanidhi here.

name: Makara Nedunkuzhaikathar Temple
significance: A Nava Tirupati Divya Desam on the Tamiraparani where the presiding lord takes his name from the makara - fish-shaped - earrings he wears, flanked by Sridevi and Bhudevi.
story: Bhudevi, cursed by the sage Durvasa, is said to have been restored when fish-shaped earrings found on the riverbank were offered to Vishnu here.

name: Alwarthirunagari Perumal Temple (Adinathar)
significance: The foremost of the nine Nava Tirupati temples on the Tamiraparani and a Divya Desam, celebrated as the birthplace of Nammalvar, the greatest of the twelve Alvar saints, whose tamarind tree still stands in the temple.
story: The infant Nammalvar is said to have sat silent in meditation in a hollow of the temple tamarind for sixteen years, until the poet Madhurakavi's riddle drew out his voice.

name: Srivilliputhur Andal Temple
builtDisplay: 8th c. core; Andal shrine and gopuram 14th-15th c.
significance: A twin-shrined Divya Desam holding Vatapatrasayi, attested from the 8th century, alongside Andal, whose 14th-century shrine and towering 192-foot rajagopuram were raised under Vijayanagara kings. It is revered as the birthplace of the Alvars Periyalvar and his foster-daughter Andal.
story: Andal is said to have been found as a baby beneath a tulasi plant and to have secretly worn the temple garlands before they were offered - a practice the deity himself endorsed in a dream.

name: Ninra Narayana Perumal Temple
significance: A hillock Divya Desam adjoining Sivakasi built by the Pandya king Devendra Vallabha, with inscriptions from the 8th century; the standing Narayana is flanked by his three consorts and sung in the Divya Prabandham.
story: Sridevi is said to have performed penance here until Vishnu appeared and stayed - 'thangal' - beside her, naming the town.

name: Kallalagar Temple (Thirumaliruncholai)
builtDisplay: attested from Sangam literature (3rd c. CE)
significance: The forest-hill Divya Desam of Thirumaliruncholai north-east of Madurai, mentioned in Sangam literature from the 3rd century CE. Each Chithirai festival the deity rides toward Madurai and enters the Vaigai river amid one of Tamil Nadu's largest festive gatherings.
story: Kallalagar is said to journey to Thenur to free the sage Suthapas of Durvasa's frog-curse - the ride his Chithirai procession re-enacts every year.

name: Thirumohoor Kalamegaperumal Temple
significance: A Divya Desam near Madurai identified in an inscription of 1259 CE under the later Pandyas, its present structure raised by the Madurai Nayaks; among the 108 shrines it is unique for the Lord's rare Prathanasayana appearance.
story: During the churning of the ocean of milk, Vishnu is said to have become the enchantress Mohini here to deny the asuras the nectar - hence Thiru-mohur.

name: Sowmyanarayana Perumal Temple
significance: A Divya Desam remembered as the place where Ramanuja, defying his teacher's restriction, proclaimed the secret liberating mantra from the temple to everyone regardless of caste.
story: Before Narasimha slew Hiranyakashipu, the gods are said to have gathered in council here, where Vishnu showed himself standing, seated and reclining.

name: Thirumittakode Anchumoorthi Temple (Thiruvithuvakkodu)
significance: The Divya Desam of Thiruvithuvakkodu on the Bharathappuzha, also counted among the 108 Shivalayams, where riverside last rites are performed as at Varanasi; the temple preserves a record of the Chola emperor Rajendra I.
story: The elephant-king Gajendra and Lakshmi are both said to have worshipped Vishnu here with lotuses from the temple's lotus garden.

name: Adikesava Perumal Temple
significance: A grand reclining-Vishnu Divya Desam encircled by three rivers, hymned from the 7th-8th centuries and once the state temple of Travancore; Vijayanagara kings added its sculpted Virabhadra columns in the early 1500s.
story: Adikesava is said to have vanquished the demon Kesi, whose widow's flood-prayer bent the rivers into the loop that rings the shrine.

name: Thiruvaragunamangai Perumal Temple
significance: One of the nine Nava Tirupati Divya Desams on the Tamiraparani, ranked next to Alwarthirunagari in importance among the nine.
story: The sage Vedavit, guided by Vishnu in the guise of a brahmin, is said to have won the Lord's abiding presence here as Vijayasanan.

name: Thirupuliyangudi Perumal Temple
significance: A Nava Tirupati Divya Desam where the reclining lord is hailed as Bhumipalar, the guardian of the earth goddess, glorified in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
story: When the slighted Bhudevi withdrew into the netherworld and the earth decayed, Vishnu is said to have descended here to win her back.

name: Koodal Azhagar Temple
significance: The city-centre Divya Desam of Madurai, believed to be a Pandya foundation later expanded by 16th-century Vijayanagara and Nayak rulers, distinguished by its rare three-tiered Ashtanga vimana.
story: Koodal Azhagar is said to have slain the demon Somuka and recovered the four Vedas stolen from Brahma.

name: Adi Jagannatha Perumal Temple
deity: Adi Jagannatha Perumal (Vishnu), with Padmasini Thayar
significance: One of the 108 Divya Desams glorified in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham, standing near the Sethu coast in Ramanathapuram district. Believed to date to the late 8th century, it was enlarged over the centuries by Chola, Pandya, Nayak and Sethupathi rulers.
story: Rama is said to have lain on darbha grass here, performing penance to compel the ocean to yield him a path to Lanka.

name: Sathyamurthi Perumal Temple
significance: A 9th-century Pallava rock-cut shrine counted among the 108 Divya Desams, today protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. It houses one of the largest reclining (Anantasayana) Vishnu images in India.
story: The Brahmanda Purana tells that the sage Satya won a boon here that Vishnu would appear whenever wished, and a king was directed to raise the temple.

name: Shri Naimishnath Vishnu Temple
deity: Devaraja Perumal (Naimishnath Vishnu), with Pundarikavalli Thayar
significance: The Vishnu temple of the sacred Naimisha forest on the Gomti, one of the 108 Divya Desams and counted among the eight self-manifested (Swayamvyakta) Vishnu shrines. The surrounding forest is revered as the place where the Puranas were first recited to the assembled sages.
story: Indra is said to have performed penance to Vishnu at Naimisha for two thousand years to overcome the asura Vritra.

name: Narsingh Temple, Joshimath
builtDisplay: trad. founded by Adi Shankara (8th c.)
significance: The main temple of Joshimath, seat of the uttaramnaya matha founded by Adi Shankara, whose Narasimha idol is traditionally held to have been installed by the acharya himself. It is revered among the 108 Vishnu shrines sung by the Tamil Alvar saints.
story: The idol's left wrist grows ever thinner; when it finally breaks, the Nar and Narayan mountains are to merge and Badrinath will reappear as a black stone at Bhavishya Badri.

name: Raghunath Temple, Devprayag
significance: A Rama temple of the 108 Divya Desams standing above the confluence where the Alaknanda and Bhagirathi unite to form the Ganga. Traditionally established by Adi Shankara, with evidence of existence by the 9th-10th century and later Garhwal royal expansion.
story: Rama is believed to have done penance here to cleanse himself of the sin of slaying Ravana, a Brahmin king.

name: Navamohana Krishna Temple
significance: The Divya Desam of Thiruvaipadi (Aypadi) at Gokul on the Yamuna, regarded as the scene of Krishna's childhood among the cowherds and sung by several Alvars including Andal. The present small shrine is a modern replacement for an older temple lost to political upheavals.
story: Here Krishna is said to have danced upon the subdued serpent Kaliya in the Yamuna before the people of Gokul.

name: Ahobilam Narasimha Temples
significance: A pilgrimage complex of nine Narasimha shrines spread over Upper and Lower Ahobilam in the Nallamala hills, revered as a canonical Divya Desam sung in the Periya Tirumoli. Its temples took their present form under Vijayanagara patronage, notably of the Saluva and Tuluva dynasties including Krishnadevaraya.

name: Tiruvetkalam Pasupatheswarar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam revered in Sambandar's Tevaram hymns, today standing within the Annamalai University campus near Chidambaram. The Chola-built complex was renovated in 1914 by a Chettiar patron.
story: Arjuna is said to have won the Pasupatha weapon here after Shiva tested him in the guise of a hunter.

name: Sivapuri Uchinathar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Tevaram canon, counted third in the series of shrines on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The temple fell into disrepair and was rebuilt in the early twentieth century.
story: The boy-saint Sambandar, travelling to his own wedding, is said to have been miraculously fed here and praised Shiva as Uchinathar.

name: Tirukkazhippalai Palvannanathar Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine of the Paadal Petra Sthalam canon near Chidambaram, revered in the 7th-century Tevaram hymns of the Nayanmars. Its lord bears the name 'the milk-hued one'.
story: A king's horse is said to have split the lingam with its hoof, and the wound was healed by milk poured by the celestial cow Kamadhenu.

name: Achalpuram Shivalokathyagar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam glorified in the Tevaram, held sacred as the place where the child-saint Sambandar ended his earthly life. Tradition places his wedding here, after which he and the assembly merged into the divine light.
story: Saint Sambandar's spirit is believed to have merged with Shiva at this shrine on his wedding day.

name: Mahendrapalli Tirumeni Azhagar Temple
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, its 'beautiful-bodied lord' praised by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram. The shrine stands near the Kollidam in Mayiladuthurai district.
story: Mahendra is believed to have worshipped Shiva here, giving the village its name.

name: Mullaivananathar Temple
deity: Mullaivana Nathar (Shiva), with Ani Konda Kothai Ammai
significance: A coastal Paadal Petra Sthalam on the northern bank of the Kaveri delta, glorified by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram. Its construction is traditionally credited to the Early Chola king Killivalavan.
story: The goddess of the shrine is herself said to have received her initiation at this place.

name: Sayavaneswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine of the Tevaram canon beside the ancient port of Kaveripoompattinam, dating from the Medieval Chola period. It is counted among the six temples held equal in sanctity to Kasi.

name: Pallavaneswarar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam at the archaeological site of Poompuhar, the drowned Sangam-era port city, and the birthplace of the saint-poet Pattinathar. It is glorified in the Tevaram hymns of Tirugnanasambandar.
story: A Pallava king is believed to have attained salvation at this shrine.

name: Swetharanyeswarar Temple
significance: The 'white forest' shrine, a Paadal Petra Sthalam and one of the nine Navagraha temples, dedicated to Budha (Mercury). Founded under the Cholas, whose inscriptions survive alongside Pandya and Vijayanagara records, its present masonry is 16th-century Vijayanagara work.
story: Shiva is said to have taken the fierce form of Aghoramurthi beneath a tree here to destroy the demon Maruthuvasuran.

name: Velladainatha Swami Temple
deity: Velladainatha Swami (Shiva as Somaskanda), with Kaviaganni
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam where Shiva is worshipped in the Somaskanda form, with attendant shrines of Ganesha, Durga and Murugan. Its glory was sung by the Saivite saints in the medieval Tevaram poems.
story: The saint Sundarar is believed to have been cleansed of sin at Thirukkurukavur after his victory in debate over the Jains.

name: Sattainathar Temple, Sirkazhi
deity: Sattainathar / Brahmapureeswarar (Shiva in three forms), with Thirunilainayaki
significance: A vast three-tiered Paadal Petra Sthalam where Shiva is worshipped on three levels as Brahmapureeswarar, Toniappar and the Bhairava form Sattainathar. The shrine of the Nayanmar age was greatly enlarged by the later Cholas from Kulothunga I to Kulothunga III, and is the storied birthplace of the saint Sambandar's devotion.
story: When the infant Sambandar cried at the temple tank, Parvati herself nursed him, and he burst forth with the first hymn of the Tevaram.

name: Vaitheeswaran Koil
deity: Vaidyanathar (Shiva, the divine healer), with Thaiyalnayagi
significance: The temple of Shiva as the 'god of healing', a Paadal Petra Sthalam and one of the nine Navagraha temples, associated with Mars (Angaraka). Inscriptions run from Kulothunga Chola I, with later endowments by Pandya, Nayak and Maratha rulers.
story: The planet-god Angaraka, stricken with leprosy, is said to have been cured here by Vaidyanatha, and so the shrine became his Navagraha seat.

name: Sivalokanathar Temple, Tirupunkur
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam a few miles west of Vaitheeswaran Koil, remembered above all for the Dalit saint Nandanar, one of the 63 Nayanmars. The shrine stands in Tamil tradition as an emblem of devotion crossing caste barriers.
story: At Shiva's command the Nandi before the sanctum moved aside so that Nandanar, barred at the gate, could behold the lord.

name: Thiruneedur Somanathaswami Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the Kaveri's northern bank, its lord praised in the Tevaram by Tirunavukkarasar and Sundarar. The temple is documented among the Later Chola foundations of the Kulottunga I to Rajendra III era.
story: A demon reborn as a crab for his sins is said to have sought liberation here on the sage Narada's counsel.

name: Kalyanasundareswarar Temple, Thiruvelvikudi
significance: A Kaveri-bank Paadal Petra Sthalam venerated in the Tevaram hymns of Sambandar and Sundarar. Tradition associates the shrine with the Ardhanarisvara form, in which Shiva shared half his body with Parvati.
story: The saint Sundarar is said to have bathed in the Agni theertham here to be cured of his illness.

name: Tirumanancheri Udhvaganathar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the Kaveri, sung by Sambandar and Tirunavukkarasar, and famed across Tamil Nadu as the 'wedding place' of Shiva. Devotees seeking marriage flock to its Kalyanasundareswarar shrine.

name: Korukkai Veeratteswarar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam and one of the eight Ashta Veeratta shrines commemorating Shiva's deeds of valour, here the subduing of Kama, the god of desire. The 9th-century Chola structure was later expanded by the Thanjavur Nayaks.
story: The sage Theerthapahu, whose hands withered for slighting the temple's sacred water, is said to have been made whole by Shiva after penance.

name: Karuppariyalur Kutram Poruttha Naathar Temple
deity: Kutram Poruttha Naathar (Shiva who forgives faults), with Kolvalai Naayaki
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam whose lord bears the name 'he who bears with transgressions' (Aparadhakshameswarar). The shrine was hymned by Tirugnanasambandar and Sundarar in the Tevaram.

name: Keezhaiyur Kadaimudinathar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the northern bank of the Kaveri near Poompuhar, glorified by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram poems.
story: Brahma himself is believed to have worshipped Shiva at this shrine.

name: Mela Kadambur Amirthakadeswarar Temple
significance: A rare karakkoil — a temple sculpted as a festival chariot, its vimana shaped like a wheeled car — built under emperor Kulottunga Chola I. It is the 88th Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Tirunavukkarasar and Sundarar.
story: Indra is said to have sought to carry the shrine to heaven, but Ganesha pinned its chariot wheel to the earth so the lord would remain for worship here.

name: Kanattampuliyur Pathanchalinathar Temple
deity: Pathanchalinathar / Patanjaleeswarar (Shiva), with Kola Valai Kai Ambicai
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Nava Puliyur group of nine 'tiger-town' shrines, glorified by Sundarar in the Tevaram. It is held to be a dwelling place of the sage Patanjali.
story: The sages Patanjali and Vyaghrapada are believed to have worshipped Shiva at this Puliyur.

name: Sakshinatheswarar Temple, Thiruppurambiyam
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam at the site of the 9th-century Battle of Thirupurambiyam, whose outcome opened the way for the Chola resurgence under Aditya I, builder of an early shrine here. The present masonry structure is 16th-century Nayak work, and the site ranks among the noted centres of Dakshinamurthy worship.
story: Shiva is said to have descended as a witness for a Chettiar lady in a dispute, earning the name Sakshinathar, 'the lord who bore witness'.

name: Vijayamangai Vijayanatheswarar Temple
significance: A Medieval Chola temple of the 'lord of victory', counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams and hymned by Tirugnanasambandar and Tirunavukkarasar.
story: Shiva is said to have granted Arjuna the Pasupata weapon here after both shot the demon Mookasura during Arjuna's penance.

name: Thiruvisanallur Sivayoginathar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the Kaveri's northern bank whose oldest masonry was raised in the reign of Parantaka I, with 16th-century Thanjavur Nayak expansions. Its early Chola sculpture, including powerfully carved vyalas, is noted by art historians.
story: A king of Kerala is said to have worshipped here to be freed of a curse incurred by mistreating women.

name: Kodeeswarar Temple, Kottaiyur
significance: A granite Paadal Petra Sthalam on the western outskirts of Kumbakonam, revered in the 7th-century Tevaram. The temple takes part in the Mahamaham festival held in Kumbakonam every twelve years.
story: Suruchi, cursed into a demon's form, is said to have regained his own after bathing in the temple's sacred spring.

name: Innambur Ezhutharinathar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam near Kumbakonam whose sanctum carries a rare Gajaprashta (elephant-back) vimana over a self-manifested lingam. The shrine is glorified in the early medieval Tevaram poems.
story: Shiva, 'the lord who knows writing', is said to have submitted the temple accounts to the king himself to save a devoted accountant from punishment.

name: Prananadeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Thirumangalakudi near Kumbakonam with a five-tiered gopuram, counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams hymned by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. It is one of the few places in South India where the Kaali Attam dance is performed, and its goddess Mangalambigai is invoked for the welfare of married women.
story: A minister of Kulothunga Chola, executed for building the temple with tax money, is said to have revived here through Mangalambigai's grace when his funeral bier reached the shrine.

name: Agniswarar Temple
significance: Shiva temple northeast of Kumbakonam revered in Appar's Tevaram and counted among the nine Navagraha temples of Tamil Nadu as the shrine of Sukra (Venus), whom devotees propitiate here against the planet's malefic effects. Built by the medieval Cholas and renovated under Vijayanagar, it has a five-tiered rajagopuram and two prakarams.
story: Shiva is said to have blessed the sage Parasara with a vision of his cosmic dance at this place, and Sukra is believed to reside within the body of the presiding deity.

name: Dayanidheeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine on the Kaveri in Thanjavur district praised by Sambandar in the Tevaram, and one of the 88 temples of the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department.
story: Hanuman, travelling south along the Kaveri with Rama, is said to have installed the Dayanidhi lingam here, giving the village its name, "the river-forest of the northern monkey".

name: Karkadeswarar Temple
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, glorified in the early medieval Tevaram by Tirugnanasambandar; the shrine near Thiruvisanallur is known as the "crab temple" (karkadam) from its founding legend.
story: A gandharva cursed by Durvasa to live as a crab worshipped the lingam here, and when Indra struck at it a hole opened in the lingam to shelter the creature.

name: Satyagireeswarar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam at Senganur (Seynjalur) glorified by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram and mentioned in Sekkizhar's Periyapuranam; it is also counted among the seven Saptha Vigraha shrines arrayed around the Mahalingaswamy temple of Thiruvidaimarudur.

name: Apathsahayar Temple
significance: Reckoned among the earliest Chola temples, this Paadal Petra Sthalam near Thiruvaiyaru is revered in the 7th-century Tevaram and belongs to the Saptha Sthanam group of shrines; its masonry spans the 9th-century Cholas to 16th-century Nayak and Vijayanagar additions.
story: When the son of the devotee Apoothi Adigal died of snakebite while cutting plantain leaves for Appar, the saint's prayer to Apathsahayar ("helper in danger") restored the boy to life.

name: Aiyarappar Temple
significance: The great Shiva temple of Thiruvaiyaru, "the place of five rivers", a Paadal Petra Sthalam revered by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar, spreading over some 60,000 square metres with four gopurams and five prakarams. Chola queens added the Uttarakailasam and Dakshinakailasam shrines, and Nayak-era work extended the complex to the 16th century.
story: Nandi is believed to have been born here to the sage Salandha and bathed by five sacred waters, and Appar is said to have been granted a vision of Mount Kailasa at this shrine.

name: Neyyadiappar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam near Thiruvaiyaru revered in the Tevaram and counted among the seven Saptha Sthanam temples of the Aiyarappar circuit. Built by Aditya Chola I in the 9th century, it preserves an inscription of AD 862 from the reign of the Pandya king Marajadaiyan.
story: A cow poured its ghee daily over a buried lingam; when the spot was dug up the lingam was found and the lord was named Neyyadiappar, "the lord bathed in ghee".

name: Vyakrapureeswarar Temple
significance: A north-bank Kaveri shrine in Thanjavur district, one of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams glorified by Tirugnanasambandar, and counted among the Nava Puliyur ("nine tiger-town") temples associated with the sages Patanjali and Vyaghrapada.

name: Vaidyanathaswami Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the north bank of the Kaveri in Ariyalur district, glorified in the Tevaram; it is famed for its annual wedding festival of Nandikesvarar and houses the largest bronze statue of the poet-saint Thiruvalluvar in Tamil Nadu, cast from 750 kg of metal.

name: Alanduraiyar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam at Kilpaluvur in Ariyalur district associated with the 7th-century saint Tirugnanasambandar; the ancient brick shrine was rebuilt in stone during the reigns of Parantaka Chola II and Uttama Chola.
story: Parasurama is believed to have worshipped here to be rid of the sin of slaying his mother.

name: Semmeninathar Temple
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams built on the northern bank of the Kaveri in Thanjavur district, glorified in the Tevaram hymns of Tirugnanasambandar and Tirunavukkarasar (Appar).

name: Sathyavaheesvarar Temple
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the banks of the Kollidam near Lalgudi, venerated in the Tevaram of Sambandar and Appar; the temple, attributed to Parantaka Chola I, has a five-tiered gopuram, three prakarams and notable images of Dakshinamurthy and Brahma.
story: When floods kept the boy-saint Sambandar on the far bank, Ganesha bent forward to hear his hymns, earning the name Sevi Saitha Vinayagar, "the Vinayaka who lent his ear".

name: Neelivaneswarar Temple
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, about 20 km north of Tiruchirappalli, with a shrine ascribed to Mahendravarman I (c. 640 CE) and inscriptions of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I. Known as Thenkailasam, it draws unmarried devotees seeking spouses and preserves a venerated plantain tree and Rathina Sabha.
story: In a contest of strength between Vayu and Adisesha, eight fragments of Mount Kailasa were scattered across the south, and Thiruppainjeeli's white hill (Suwethagiri) is held to be one of them.

name: Mattrurai Varadeswarar Temple
significance: One of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, at Thiruvasi near Tiruchirappalli, celebrated in the Tevaram hymns of Tirugnanasambandar and Sundarar; the site was anciently known as Tirupachilasramam.

name: Jambukeswarar Temple, Thiruvanaikaval
significance: One of the five Pancha Bhoota Sthalams of Shiva, embodying the element water — an underground stream keeps the sanctum lingam perpetually wet — and also a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The vast complex carries 11th–12th-century Chola inscriptions and was greatly expanded, with its seven-tiered rajagopuram, by the Hoysala king Someswara in 1236–37.
story: Parvati, doing penance on earth, fashioned a lingam of water beneath a jambu tree, where two cursed celestials worshipped it as an elephant and a spider until their devotion freed them.

name: Maragadachaleswarar Temple
significance: A hilltop Paadal Petra Sthalam above the Kaveri in Tiruchirappalli district, glorified by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram, and counted among the eight sites believed to hold fragments of Mount Kailasa.
